analysis.one_liner: Offered Senate candidates full public financing in exchange for collecting small $5 donations from voters instead of large checks from donors.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in May 2007, the bill got a single Senate committee hearing in June and died without ever coming to a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Elections Now Act would have let Senate candidates opt into a public financing system. A candidate who collected enough small $5 contributions from state residents would receive grants from a new Senate Fair Elections Fund, discounted TV and radio ad rates, and ad vouchers — and in exchange would give up large private contributions and most spending from personal wealth. The fund would be filled mostly by proceeds from federal spectrum auctions and a fee on broadcasters' advertising revenue, not by ordinary income taxes. The bill also cut back the congressional free-mailing (franking) privilege in the 90 days before elections. It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, got one hearing, and never received a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates for the Senate without personal wealth or access to big donors — they could qualify for full campaign funding by collecting thousands of $5 contributions from their own state's residents instead of courting large donors. Voters gain more competitive races and candidates less dependent on the interests that fund campaigns; taxpayers could benefit indirectly if the bill's own findings are right that privately financed elections skew legislation toward contributors [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Candidates without wealth or big donors

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who chose the program received grants for the primary and general elections — $750,000 plus $150,000 per additional congressional district, adjusted for media costs and inflation — funded largely by spectrum auction proceeds and fees on broadcasters rather than by ordinary taxpayers [S2, S3].
If an opponent or outside groups outspent a participating candidate, the candidate received matching 'fair fight' funds to keep the race competitive [S3].
Participating candidates got reduced broadcast advertising rates and vouchers for political ads, lowering the single biggest cost of running statewide [S2, S3].

The bill barred Senators from sending franked (taxpayer-funded) mass mailings in the 90 days before elections unless they were not running for re-election, closing a channel through which incumbents used public money to reach voters at campaign time [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broadcast TV and radio stations pay most directly — a spectrum use fee equal to 2% of their gross advertising revenue, required discounts of up to 20% off the lowest ad rates for participating candidates, and audits of their ad pricing [S3]. Large donors and lobbying interests lose the influence that comes from financing campaigns, and Senators lose the use of taxpayer-funded mass mailings in the 90 days before an election [S3]. Ordinary taxpayers are largely shielded: the fund draws on spectrum auction proceeds, the broadcaster fee, and the $5 qualifying contributions themselves [S3].

drawbacks.text: Public campaign money has to come from somewhere: the bill redirected 10% of federal spectrum auction proceeds into the fund and imposed a fee on broadcasters' gross advertising revenue, and the Fair Elections Review Commission was authorized to seek appropriations [S3].

Participating candidates agreed to forgo ordinary private contributions and largely fund campaigns from fixed allocations, and fair fight money was capped at 200% of the allocation — so a candidate facing heavy spending by outside groups could end up outgunned despite the matching funds [S3].

The bill itself acknowledged legal risk: it contained a severability clause and a dedicated section on review of constitutional issues, reflecting that court challenges to the spending and speech provisions were anticipated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside was real: a candidate who chose the program got enough money to run a competitive Senate race by collecting $5 donations from neighbors instead of courting large donors, plus discounted airtime and matching money when outspent [S3]. The costs are honest ones: funding had to come from somewhere — here mostly spectrum proceeds and fees on broadcasters rather than general taxes — and no one could guarantee the grants would keep pace with ever-rising TV costs even with indexing [S3]. A candidate who took public money accepted spending discipline while unbound outside groups faced no limits, so the bill traded one influence problem for another to some degree. And constitutional uncertainty was acknowledged in the bill itself [S3]. Still, the mechanism was voluntary and audited, and the main objection — cost to taxpayers — was substantially defrayed by the spectrum funding design. The larger cost was never tested: the bill died before any chamber could debate it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, got one hearing in June 2007, and the committee never voted to send it to the floor, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Durbin introduced the bill on May 3, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration [S1, S5].
The committee held hearings on June 20, 2007 — the only action the bill ever received beyond its referral [S5].
No committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call ever occurred; the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent senators and the existing donor network were the direct beneficiaries, since privately financed Senate campaigns continued unchanged; broadcast stations were spared the advertising fee and rate cuts.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois (Assistant Majority Leader)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 3, 2007 and was its lead sponsor [S1, S3, S5].

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, the bill's only Republican supporter [S3, S4].

for.name: Sens. Russ Feingold and Barack Obama
for.role: U.S. Senators from Wisconsin and Illinois
for.what_they_did: Joined Durbin and Specter as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced [S3].

for.name: 8 Senate Democrats and 1 Senate Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — nine senators in total, eight Democrats and one Republican [S4].

for.name: Common Cause and Public Campaign
for.what_they_did: Long championed public financing of congressional elections and promoted the Fair Elections Now Act during this period.

against.name: Dianne Feinstein
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill, held a single hearing on June 20, 2007, and never reported it out or scheduled any vote [S5].

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Widely known to control the Senate floor schedule as Majority Leader; the bill never received floor consideration during his tenure in the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — nine cosponsors including one Republican, Arlen Specter, joining lead Democrat Dick Durbin [S4] — but because no vote was ever held, the partisan shape of actual support and opposition never appeared on the record.

industries.note: The bill charged stations a spectrum use fee equal to 2% of gross advertising revenue, required participating candidates be charged no more than 80% of the lowest ad rate, barred preemption of paid candidate ads, and created audits of ad pricing [S3]. Political advertising is a major revenue stream for broadcasters, so this came directly out of their business.

industries.industry: Major private donors and lobbying firms
industries.note: Participating candidates had to give up private contributions beyond small seed money and $5 qualifying donations, shrinking the currency of access that large donors and lobbying firms rely on [S3]. Nothing in the record shows these actors acting on the bill, but the mechanism runs squarely against their role.

The franking restriction cut off taxpayer-funded mass mailings in the 90 days before elections for members running for re-election, and the fundraising program reduced dependence on the donor networks incumbents traditionally dominate [S3].
